effect: A currency reform now cuts household loans by the same share as household deposits. When a currency is reformed (the deflation-trap or hyperinflation reform, MTa and Ryt), the game takes 85% of each household's main deposit (vjt, householdDepositHaircut01) and books it to the bank as resolution income, while every household loan stays whole: savers lose most of their money, borrowers owe as much as before, and the bank keeps the difference. Now, after the deposit cut, each household loan of the reformed country is written down by the same share through the game's own loan write-off (g8e: the bank's credit-loss expense against the loan asset, the household's loan liability against debt-forgiveness income), so both sides of the household balance sheet are converted at one rate. The loan's repayment schedule shrinks with it: its original principal (and, for a mortgage, both original parts), its monthly amortisation and its accrued interest are scaled by the same factor as the outstanding principal, so the monthly instalment falls in proportion and the loan still ends on its original date (the game bills principal as original principal / maturity, TH, so without this a cut loan would still demand the pre-reform instalment). A mortgage whose outstanding parts do not add up to the loan (an invariant the game's own write-off checks and throws on, gB) is skipped with a console warning instead of stopping the reform half-applied. Real-world behaviour: the aim is whatever is closest to real life. Conversions that cut money claims convert debts with them: the West German currency reform of June 1948 converted savings and private debts together (most at 10 to 1, the banks' balance sheets closed by state equalisation claims), and modern redenominations (Turkey 2005, Romania 2005, Ghana 2007, Venezuela 2008, 2018 and 2021) convert deposits and loans at the same rate. Reforms that only froze or confiscated deposits (Soviet Union 1991, Brazil 1990) did not leave household debts whole in a way that handed the gain to banks. The bank's result is now the gain on deposits minus the loss on loans, with no equalisation claim (the game has none), so a bank whose household loans exceed its household deposits can lose, and the game's own solvency test then applies (g8e marks it insolvent), as for any write-off. Company deposits, foreign-currency accounts and company loans are unchanged, as in the game. Crisis path only: no day-0 effect. No new state.
